title: LRU cache (and LFU)
scopeHtml: Scope: LRU cache with O(1) get/put, thread-safe wrapper, LFU follow-up, runnable Java and Kotlin. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a fixed-size cache that throws away the "least recently used" entry when full, with O(1) get and put. Then extend it to LFU (least frequently used).

Ask these before coding: is it generic (any key and value types)? Fixed capacity? What do get of a missing key and put of an existing key do? Does it need to be thread-safe? Is there a TTL? (Here: generic, fixed capacity, get returns null on miss, put on an existing key updates and refreshes it, thread-safety as a follow-up, no TTL.)

Worked example. Capacity 2. put(a), put(b), get(a), put(c). After get(a), a is the freshest and b the stalest, so put(c) evicts b. A naive "scan for the oldest timestamp" costs O(n) per eviction; with a 1M-entry cache and 50k puts/s that is 50 billion steps/s, impossible. We need O(1).

Industry examples. Guava CacheBuilder, Caffeine (uses W-TinyLFU, a smarter LFU/LRU mix), Redis maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (approximate LRU: samples a few keys, evicts the oldest of the sample, to save memory), Android android.util.LruCache for bitmaps, the Linux page cache.

Everyday analogy. A small desk that fits 5 books. When you need a 6th, you put back the one you have not touched for longest.

Common interview traps.

  • Using only a HashMap plus timestamps (O(n) eviction).
  • Using LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true) and stopping there. It is a valid shortcut (override removeEldestEntry), mention it, but the interviewer usually wants you to build the list yourself.
  • Forgetting that get changes state (recency), which matters for thread safety later.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
Three pieces only:

  • Cache<K,V> interface: get, put, size. Callers depend on this, so LRU, LFU and a thread-safe wrapper are interchangeable.
  • Node: holds key, value, prev, next. The key is stored in the node so that when we evict the tail we know which map entry to delete.
  • HashMap<K, Node> for O(1) lookup, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency (head = freshest, tail = stalest).

Why both? A map finds a node in O(1) but has no order. A list keeps order and removes a known node in O(1) (if doubly linked) but cannot find one without scanning. Together: find via map, reorder via list.

Decision gravity. The data-structure choice is internal behind the Cache interface, so it is reversible (a two-way door). The interface itself is the one to get right early because many callers depend on it.

Everyday analogy. A library index (map) tells you which shelf slot a book is in; the shelf itself (list) is where you move the book you just used to the front.

Common interview traps.

  • A singly linked list: removing a node from the middle needs its predecessor, which is O(n).
  • Not storing the key in the node, so eviction cannot remove the map entry.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
<<interface>>
   +--------------------+
   |  Cache<K,V>        |
   |  get(K): V         |
   |  put(K,V)          |
   |  size(): int       |
   +--------------------+
      ^         ^          ^
      |         |          |
+-----------+ +-----------+ +--------------------+
| LRUCache  | | LFUCache  | | SynchronizedCache  |
| map       | | vals      | | inner: Cache  -----+--> wraps any Cache
| head,tail | | freq      | | (Decorator)        |
| capacity  | | buckets   | +--------------------+
+-----------+ | minFreq   |
   | has many +-----------+
   v
+---------------------+
| Node: key,val,prev, |
|       next          |
+---------------------+

List order:  head <-> [freshest] <-> ... <-> [stalest] <-> tail

How to read it. head and tail are dummy sentinel nodes, so inserting and removing never needs null checks. The real LRU victim is always tail.prev.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the sentinels; the code then fills with if (head == null) branches.
  • Making LRUCache itself synchronized. Better to keep it simple and wrap it (Decorator) so single-threaded users pay nothing.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Decorator (SynchronizedCache): adds locking around any Cache without changing it. Why: thread safety is a separate concern; single-threaded callers should not pay. Alternative: put synchronized inside LRUCache (simpler, cannot be turned off). Breaks when one global lock becomes the bottleneck (see Concurrency). Reversible.
  • Strategy (eviction policy): LRU and LFU are two policies behind one interface. In a bigger design you would split EvictionPolicy (onAccess, evict) from storage so a Guava-style cache can swap policy by config. Not done here: for one interview, two classes are clearer than three abstractions.
  • Sentinel nodes: removes edge cases; a coding technique, not a GoF pattern.

Industry examples. Caffeine and Guava build an eviction policy + storage + stats + loader pipeline; Redis picks a policy via config; the JDK's own LinkedHashMap is the built-in LRU.

Everyday analogy. A bouncer (decorator) in front of a club: the club (cache) works the same; the bouncer only lets one person through the door at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming patterns without saying what problem each solves.
  • Adding an EvictionPolicy hierarchy, a CacheBuilder and a StatsCounter in a 45-minute round. Offer them as extensions instead.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (LRU, synchronized wrapper, LFU and a test in main):

import java.util.*;

interface Cache<K, V> {
    V get(K key);
    void put(K key, V value);
    int size();
}

/** O(1) get/put: HashMap for lookup + doubly linked list for recency order. NOT thread-safe. */
class LRUCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {
    private class Node {
        K key; V val; Node prev, next;
        Node(K k, V v) { key = k; val = v; }
    }
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node head = new Node(null, null), tail = new Node(null, null); // sentinels

    LRUCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail; tail.prev = head;
    }
    public V get(K key) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n == null) return null;
        unlink(n); addFront(n);              // a read makes it most recent
        return n.val;
    }
    public void put(K key, V value) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n != null) { n.val = value; unlink(n); addFront(n); return; }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {        // evict least recently used = node before tail
            Node lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key);
        }
        n = new Node(key, value);
        map.put(key, n); addFront(n);
    }
    public int size() { return map.size(); }
    private void unlink(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
    private void addFront(Node n) {
        n.next = head.next; n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n; head.next = n;
    }
}

/** Thread-safe decorator: get() mutates order, so even reads need the lock. */
class SynchronizedCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {
    private final Cache<K, V> inner;
    SynchronizedCache(Cache<K, V> inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    public synchronized V get(K key) { return inner.get(key); }
    public synchronized void put(K key, V value) { inner.put(key, value); }
    public synchronized int size() { return inner.size(); }
}

/** LFU follow-up, O(1): key->value, key->freq, freq->keys in insertion order, plus minFreq. */
class LFUCache<K, V> implements Cache<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, V> vals = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<K, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<Integer, LinkedHashSet<K>> buckets = new HashMap<>();
    private int minFreq = 0;

    LFUCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }
    public V get(K key) {
        if (!vals.containsKey(key)) return null;
        touch(key);
        return vals.get(key);
    }
    public void put(K key, V value) {
        if (vals.containsKey(key)) { vals.put(key, value); touch(key); return; }
        if (vals.size() == capacity) {       // evict lowest freq; ties -> oldest (LRU) in that bucket
            LinkedHashSet<K> set = buckets.get(minFreq);
            K victim = set.iterator().next();
            set.remove(victim);
            vals.remove(victim); freq.remove(victim);
        }
        vals.put(key, value); freq.put(key, 1);
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(1, f -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
        minFreq = 1;
    }
    public int size() { return vals.size(); }
    private void touch(K key) {
        int f = freq.get(key);
        LinkedHashSet<K> set = buckets.get(f);
        set.remove(key);
        if (set.isEmpty() && minFreq == f) minFreq = f + 1;
        freq.put(key, f + 1);
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(f + 1, x -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
    }
}

public class Main {
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Cache<String, Integer> lru = new LRUCache<>(2);
        lru.put("a", 1); lru.put("b", 2);
        lru.get("a");                 // a is now most recent
        lru.put("c", 3);              // evicts b
        check(lru.get("b") == null && lru.get("a") == 1 && lru.get("c") == 3, "LRU eviction");

        Cache<String, Integer> lfu = new LFUCache<>(2);
        lfu.put("a", 1); lfu.put("b", 2);
        lfu.get("a"); lfu.get("a");   // a freq 3, b freq 1
        lfu.put("c", 3);              // evicts b (lowest freq)
        check(lfu.get("b") == null && lfu.get("a") == 1, "LFU eviction");

        // concurrency: 8 threads hammer a synchronized cache; size must never exceed capacity
        Cache<Integer, Integer> safe = new SynchronizedCache<>(new LRUCache<>(100));
        Thread[] ts = new Thread[8];
        for (int t = 0; t < ts.length; t++) {
            final int id = t;
            ts[t] = new Thread(() -> {
                Random r = new Random(id);
                for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                    int k = r.nextInt(500);
                    if (r.nextBoolean()) safe.put(k, k); else safe.get(k);
                }
            });
            ts[t].start();
        }
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
        check(safe.size() <= 100, "capacity respected under contention");
        System.out.println("P7 OK, size=" + safe.size());
    }
}

The same core in Kotlin (LRU; the rest follows identically):

class LRUCache<K : Any, V>(private val capacity: Int) {
    private class Node<K, V>(val key: K?, var value: V?) {
        var prev: Node<K, V>? = null
        var next: Node<K, V>? = null
    }
    private val map = HashMap<K, Node<K, V>>()
    private val head = Node<K, V>(null, null)
    private val tail = Node<K, V>(null, null)

    init {
        require(capacity > 0)
        head.next = tail; tail.prev = head
    }

    @Synchronized fun get(key: K): V? {
        val n = map[key] ?: return null
        unlink(n); addFront(n)
        return n.value
    }

    @Synchronized fun put(key: K, value: V) {
        map[key]?.let { it.value = value; unlink(it); addFront(it); return }
        if (map.size == capacity) {
            val lru = tail.prev!!
            unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key)
        }
        val n = Node(key, value)
        map[key] = n; addFront(n)
    }

    private fun unlink(n: Node<K, V>) { n.prev!!.next = n.next; n.next!!.prev = n.prev }
    private fun addFront(n: Node<K, V>) {
        n.next = head.next; n.prev = head
        head.next!!.prev = n; head.next = n
    }
}

// Shortcut worth knowing (JVM): LinkedHashMap does exactly this
fun <K, V> lru(cap: Int) = object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) {
    override fun removeEldestEntry(e: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>) = size > cap
}

How get and put work. get: map lookup, unlink the node, add it at the front. put of a new key when full: remove tail.prev, delete its map entry, then insert the new node at the front. Each step is a handful of pointer writes, so O(1).

LFU idea. Keep a frequency per key, and for each frequency a LinkedHashSet of keys (insertion order = recency among ties). Track minFreq. Evict the oldest key of the minFreq bucket; touching a key moves it from bucket f to f+1, and if bucket minFreq became empty, minFreq++. A new key always has frequency 1, so minFreq resets to 1.

LFU state after: put a, put b, get a, get a
vals     : a=1, b=2
freq     : a=3, b=1
buckets  : 1 -> [b]     3 -> [a]
minFreq  : 1     -> put c evicts b

Common interview traps.

  • Updating an existing key without moving it to the front.
  • LFU tie-breaking left undefined; say "among equal frequency, evict the least recently used".
  • LFU with a PriorityQueue: O(log n) and stale entries; the bucket design is O(1).

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints: P7 OK, size=100

-ea enables the check assertions. The test covers: LRU evicts the right key after a get refresh; LFU evicts the lowest-frequency key; 8 threads doing 800,000 random operations never push a synchronized cache above capacity 100.

In a real project (JUnit) you would add: put on an existing key refreshes order; capacity 1; a null-value policy; an eviction callback; repeated stress runs.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "I tested it" without a walk-through. Do a dry run on the board with capacity 2 and 4 operations.
  • Not testing capacity 1 (sentinel edge case).

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The trap: get is a write. It reorders the list, so even read-only callers mutate shared state. A ReadWriteLock does not help (reads need the write lock), and a plain HashMap read concurrent with a write can corrupt it (the classic pre-Java-8 symptom: 100% CPU stuck in HashMap.get).

Three levels, simplest to best:

  1. One lock (the synchronized wrapper above). Correct and simple. Under heavy multi-thread load all callers queue on one lock, so throughput flattens at a few million ops/s.
  2. Lock striping. Hash the key to one of 16 or 64 segments, each its own small LRU with its own lock. Contention drops roughly by the segment count; the price is that LRU becomes approximate (per segment, not global). Older Guava (concurrencyLevel, default 4) worked this way.
  3. Buffered recency (Caffeine). Reads hit a ConcurrentHashMap without locking and just record the access in a lock-free buffer; a maintenance task replays those records to reorder the list. Reads become nearly lock-free. Cost: eviction order lags slightly.
// Level 2 sketch: independent shards
class ShardedCache<K, V> {
    private final Cache<K, V>[] shards;
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    ShardedCache(int n, int capPerShard) {
        shards = new Cache[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) shards[i] = new SynchronizedCache<>(new LRUCache<>(capPerShard));
    }
    private Cache<K, V> shard(K k) { return shards[(k.hashCode() & 0x7fffffff) % shards.length]; }
    V get(K k) { return shard(k).get(k); }
    void put(K k, V v) { shard(k).put(k, v); }
}

Cache stampede (a production incident). When a hot key expires, 1,000 requests miss at once and all hit the database. Symptom: DB CPU spikes right after a deploy that cleared the cache; the metric that shows it is the cache hit ratio dropping from about 98% to near 0%. Fixes: per-key single flight (first caller loads, others wait), jittered TTLs, or serve stale while refreshing (Caffeine refreshAfterWrite).

Decision gravity. Starting with one lock is correct and reversible. Moving to striping changes eviction semantics (approximate global LRU), so tell callers; treat it as a one-way-ish door if anything depends on exact order.

Everyday analogy. One cashier (single lock) versus several checkout lanes (striping). Lanes are faster, but "the single longest-waiting customer goes first" is no longer guaranteed.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "use ConcurrentHashMap" and forgetting the list must be updated atomically with the map.
  • Synchronizing only put. Both get and put mutate.
  • Holding the lock while loading from the database on a miss; loads must happen outside the lock.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• TTL expiry: store expiresAt in the Node; check lazily on get, and sweep with a scheduled task.
  • LFU frequency aging: classic LFU never forgets old popularity. TinyLFU/Caffeine halve counters periodically; Redis LFU uses a logarithmic counter that decays (lfu-decay-time).
  • Cache-aside vs read-through: a loader function (computeIfAbsent style) lets the cache fetch misses itself.
  • Write policies: write-through, write-back (risk of loss), write-around.
  • Distributed: consistent hashing across cache nodes (Memcached clients, Redis Cluster slots); see the HLD caching topics.
  • Memory limit instead of count: weigh entries by byte size (Caffeine maximumWeight).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to distributed caches before finishing the single-node version.
  • Forgetting an eviction listener when entries hold resources (file handles, bitmaps).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• LRU = HashMap for lookup + doubly linked list for order, with sentinel head/tail. All operations O(1).
  • get mutates recency, so thread safety needs the write lock even for reads; wrap with a Decorator.
  • LFU in O(1): key to freq, freq to ordered key set, plus minFreq; ties broken by recency.
  • Scale locking in steps: one lock, then striping, then buffered recency (Caffeine).
  • Mention the stampede problem and TTL jitter; they show production experience.
